tags.vr: a network with a virtual router

cards.name: Advanced zone
cards.text: The full network model: isolated networks, VPCs and shared networks.

cards.name: Basic zone
cards.text: One flat network with security groups. Simple and cheap, but no VPCs or virtual routers for tenants.

cards.name: Edge zone
cards.text: A lightweight KVM-only zone with no system VMs, for small remote sites.

cards.name: Second zone (DR site)
cards.text: Another zone in a separate data centre, so a whole site can fail.

cards.name: KVM hosts
cards.text: Open-source and the most widely used hypervisor with CloudStack. Works in every zone type.

cards.name: VMware vSphere cluster
cards.text: Familiar, mature and licensed per core. Not supported in Edge zones.

cards.name: XCP-ng pool
cards.text: Open-source Xen-based hypervisor. Not supported in Edge zones.

cards.name: Local storage
cards.text: Disks inside each host. Cheapest and fast, but data is lost if the host is.

cards.name: NFS primary storage
cards.text: Shared storage that every hypervisor understands. One NFS server is still one point of failure.

cards.name: Ceph RBD
cards.text: Distributed, replicated block storage for KVM.

cards.name: StorPool block storage
cards.text: Partner card. High-performance, replicated block storage with a native CloudStack plugin for KVM.

cards.name: LINSTOR
cards.text: Partner card. DRBD-replicated storage managed by LINSTOR, with a native CloudStack plugin for KVM.

cards.name: vSphere datastore
cards.text: A VMFS or vSAN datastore presented to the vSphere cluster.

cards.name: NFS secondary storage
cards.text: Holds templates, ISOs and volume snapshots. Edge zones download templates directly instead.

cards.name: Object storage
cards.text: S3-compatible buckets for users, backed by MinIO or Ceph.

cards.name: Isolated network
cards.text: A private network per account, with a virtual router for NAT, DHCP, firewall and load balancing.

cards.name: VPC
cards.text: Multi-tier private cloud network with ACLs between tiers.

cards.name: Security groups
cards.text: Per-VM firewall rules on a flat network.

cards.name: Shared network
cards.text: One network shared by many accounts. Quick, but no isolation between tenants.

cards.name: L2 network
cards.text: A plain VLAN with no CloudStack network services. Bring your own router.

cards.name: Redundant virtual router
cards.text: A second router in active-passive mode, so a router failure doesn't cut tenants off.

cards.name: Load balancer rules
cards.text: Spread public traffic across VMs using the virtual router.

cards.name: Site-to-site VPN
cards.text: Link a VPC to an office or another data centre over IPsec.

cards.name: Remote access VPN
cards.text: Let individual users connect into their network.

cards.name: CloudStack Kubernetes Service
cards.text: Users deploy and scale Kubernetes clusters from the CloudStack UI or API.

cards.name: AutoScale VM group
cards.text: Adds and removes VMs behind a load balancer as load changes.

cards.name: KVM Host HA
cards.text: Detects failed hosts, fences them through out-of-band management and restarts their VMs elsewhere.

cards.name: vSphere HA
cards.text: VMware's own HA restarts VMs on surviving hosts.

cards.name: XCP-ng pool HA
cards.text: The pool restarts protected VMs when a host fails.

cards.name: NAS backup
cards.text: CloudStack's built-in backup provider for KVM, writing to an NFS or CIFS share.

cards.name: Veeam backup
cards.text: Backup and restore for VMware-based zones through the Veeam provider.

cards.name: Sendense
cards.text: Partner card. Backup, recovery and workload mobility across CloudStack and mixed infrastructure.

cards.name: VMware to KVM import
cards.text: Built-in import of VMs from vCenter into KVM, converting them with virt-v2v.

cards.name: Usage server
cards.text: Records resource usage per account so you can bill customers.

cards.name: Domains and projects
cards.text: Organise customers into domains, accounts and projects with their own limits.

cards.name: LDAP / Active Directory
cards.text: Users log in with their existing directory accounts.

cards.name: SAML 2.0 single sign-on
cards.text: Log in through the company identity provider.

cards.name: GPU hosts
cards.text: KVM hosts with GPUs passed through to VMs, for AI training and virtual desktops.

cards.name: ARM64 KVM hosts
cards.text: Energy-efficient ARM servers running KVM, managed alongside x86 hosts.

cards.name: Cluster DRS
cards.text: Live-migrates VMs to even out load across the hosts in a cluster.

cards.name: Host anti-affinity groups
cards.text: Keeps the VMs of a clustered app on different hosts.

cards.name: Dedicated hosts
cards.text: Reserves hosts or clusters for a single customer's VMs.

cards.name: Volume encryption
cards.text: Encrypts VM disks at rest on KVM.

cards.name: Shared file systems
cards.text: Users create NFS shares on demand and mount them across their VMs.

cards.name: Disk offerings with IOPS limits
cards.text: Caps how much disk throughput each volume can use.

cards.name: Dell PowerFlex
cards.text: Software-defined block storage managed through a CloudStack storage plugin.

cards.name: IPv6 networks
cards.text: Gives isolated networks and VPC tiers public IPv6 addresses.

cards.name: Routed mode with BGP
cards.text: Routes tenant networks directly without NAT, announcing them to your routers over BGP.

cards.name: VNF appliance
cards.text: Deploy a network function such as a Suricata intrusion-detection appliance from a template.

cards.name: VPC private gateway
cards.text: Connects a VPC to an on-premises network over a dedicated VLAN.

cards.name: Internal load balancer
cards.text: Balances traffic between tiers inside a VPC.

cards.name: VMware NSX
cards.text: SDN for VMware-based zones. Powerful, but it ties your network to VMware.

cards.name: CloudStack Kubernetes Provider
cards.text: Cloud controller manager that gives Kubernetes LoadBalancer services a CloudStack load balancer.

cards.name: CloudStack CSI driver
cards.text: Provisions CloudStack volumes as Kubernetes persistent volumes.

cards.name: Cluster API Provider (CAPC)
cards.text: Creates and upgrades Kubernetes clusters declaratively with Cluster API.

cards.name: Terraform provider
cards.text: Define zones, networks and VMs as code and rebuild them on demand.

cards.name: Prometheus exporter
cards.text: Exposes capacity and health metrics for dashboards and alerts.

cards.name: Webhooks
cards.text: Sends CloudStack events to ticketing, chat and automation tools.

cards.name: Two-factor authentication
cards.text: Users confirm logins with a time-based code.

cards.name: OAuth2 login
cards.text: Log in with an existing Google or GitHub account.

cards.name: Custom roles
cards.text: Give each user only the API permissions their job needs.

cards.name: Quota
cards.text: Sets credit limits per account and stops spending when they run out.

scenarios.title: SaaS launch
scenarios.brief: A start-up is launching a web platform next month. Each tenant needs a private network, and traffic will spike after the press release.

scenarios.title: VMware exit
scenarios.brief: 2,000 VMs, and the vSphere licence renewal is in 90 days. Move everything to an open-source hypervisor without losing HA or backups.

scenarios.title: Hosting provider public cloud
scenarios.brief: A regional hosting company wants self-service VMs for hundreds of tenants, billed monthly, with no single router taking a tenant offline.

scenarios.title: Sovereign cloud for a bank
scenarios.brief: Data must stay in-country on open infrastructure. Auditors want a second site, backups, staff logging in with corporate accounts, and a secure link to head office.

scenarios.title: Kubernetes platform
scenarios.brief: The platform team wants developers to create their own Kubernetes clusters on isolated networks, publish apps, and store artefacts in S3 buckets.

scenarios.title: Retail edge rollout
scenarios.brief: Two small servers in each of 200 shops, managed centrally. Staff log in with head-office accounts and the till data must be backed up.

scenarios.title: AI research lab
scenarios.brief: A university wants GPU machines for its research groups, shared datasets every VM can mount, and a spending limit per group so no lab burns the whole grant.

scenarios.title: Platform engineering team
scenarios.brief: Developers want Kubernetes clusters with working LoadBalancer services and persistent volumes. Everything must be defined as code and monitored.

scenarios.title: Telco network cloud
scenarios.brief: A mobile operator is running out of IPv4 addresses. Its network functions need IPv6, intrusion detection on subscriber traffic, and no single router outage.

scenarios.title: Hospital group
scenarios.brief: Patient records need encrypted disks on hardware no one else shares. Staff need two-factor login and only the access their role requires. Downtime is not an option.

host-failure.title: A host loses power at 3 a.m.
host-failure.win: HA restarted the VMs on other hosts before anyone woke up.
host-failure.lose: VMs stayed down until someone restarted them by hand. VM high availability would have recovered them.

storage-failure.title: A storage server fails
storage-failure.win: Replicated storage kept every volume online.
storage-failure.lose: Volumes on the failed server went offline. Replicated storage such as Ceph, StorPool or LINSTOR keeps a copy elsewhere.

ransomware.title: Ransomware encrypts a tenant's VMs
ransomware.win: You restored last night's backups and the tenant was back in an hour.
ransomware.lose: With no backups, the data was gone. A backup provider would have saved it.

site-outage.title: The whole data centre goes dark
site-outage.win: Workloads came back in the second zone.
site-outage.lose: Everything was down until the site came back. A second zone gives you somewhere to recover to.

traffic-spike.title: Traffic jumps tenfold overnight
traffic-spike.win: The AutoScale group added VMs and the site stayed fast.
traffic-spike.lose: The site slowed to a crawl. An AutoScale VM group would have added capacity.

router-failure.title: A virtual router crashes
router-failure.win: The standby router took over within seconds.
router-failure.lose: Tenants lost connectivity until the router was rebuilt. A redundant virtual router avoids that.

noisy-neighbour.title: One tenant's VM hammers the shared disks
noisy-neighbour.win: IOPS limits, rebalancing or dedicated hardware kept everyone else fast.
noisy-neighbour.lose: Every other VM slowed down. IOPS limits, Cluster DRS or dedicated hosts would have contained it.

intrusion.title: An attacker scans tenant networks
intrusion.win: The intrusion-detection appliance flagged the scan and the source was blocked.
intrusion.lose: Nobody noticed until a tenant complained. An intrusion-detection VNF would have caught it.

phishing.title: An admin's password is phished
phishing.win: Without the second factor, the stolen password was useless.
phishing.lose: The attacker logged straight in. Two-factor authentication would have stopped them.

ipv4-exhaustion.title: The last public IPv4 block is used up
ipv4-exhaustion.win: New services came up on IPv6 and routed networks, with no new IPv4 needed.
ipv4-exhaustion.lose: New services had to wait for addresses. IPv6 or routed networks avoid the squeeze.

rebuild-rush.title: 50 test environments must be rebuilt by Friday
rebuild-rush.lose: The team clicked through the UI all week. Infrastructure as code would have done it in minutes.

silent-degradation.title: Disk latency creeps up for a week
silent-degradation.win: An alert fired on day one and the failing disk was replaced.
silent-degradation.lose: Nobody noticed until users complained. Monitoring would have warned you early.
